# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–23 (Complete – Updated 166)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of sixth year, afternoon of Sunday** (Chapter 23). Rawdon has discovered Rebecca with Steyne, confronted them, visited Pitt to arrange guardianship of little Rawdon, and is arranging duel with Steyne. Amelia continues evening vigils at Russell Square. Little Rawdon at school.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opened "summer of sixth year"; Chapter 23 opens "autumn of sixth year." Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph.
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Brompton Square); Queen's Crawley; and others as previously noted.

## The Catastrophic Discovery and Immediate Aftermath (Chapters 22–23)

**Rawdon's Return Home and Confrontation (Chapter 22–23)**: Found drawing-room blazing with light at nine o'clock. Found Steyne bowing to kiss Rebecca's hand; Rebecca sat in brilliant toilette, arms sparkling with bracelets given by Steyne. Rawdon seized Steyne by neckcloth, struck him twice over face with open hand, flung him bleeding to ground. Steyne wore scar to his dying day.

**Jewel and Financial Discovery (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon flung open boxes and wardrobes, found desk Amelia had given Rebecca containing papers, love-letters, trinkets, and pocket-book with bank-notes. **CRITICAL DISCOVERY**: Bank-notes including fresh note for **one thousand pounds from Lord Steyne**—evidence of extensive financial support constituting payment for sexual favors.

**Rebecca's Aftermath (Chapter 23)**: Remained alone for hours, certain "he would never come back. He was gone forever." Experienced suicidal ideation: considered laudanum. French maid (accomplice, in Steyne's pay) persuaded her to rest on bed with kindness. Maid gathered trinkets from floor. By afternoon, Rebecca awakened from stupor when Curzon Street Chapel bells rang for afternoon service. Rang for maid repeatedly, pulled down bell-rope in desperation, screamed from landing with hair loose.

**Rebecca's Revelation of Heritage (Chapter 23)**: Rebecca claimed innocence before God. Rawdon screamed: "You're as innocent as your mother, the ballet-girl, and your husband the bully." **REVELATION**: Rebecca's mother was a ballet-girl; her father (characterized by Rawdon) was a bully.

## Rawdon's Actions and Duel Arrangements (Chapter 23 – Latest)

**Morning Meeting with Pitt (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon arrived at Great Gaunt Street in evening costume worn two days, blood-shot eyed, tumbled clothes. Pitt appeared fresh and neat, initially thought Rawdon intoxicated. Pitt refused financial help: "Even the hundred pounds that Jane took you last night were promised to my lawyer to-morrow morning."

**Rawdon's Confession and Request (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon spoke in husky voice: "It's the boy. I want you to promise me that you will take charge of him when I'm gone." Rawdon revealed full circumstances of financial manipulation and Rebecca's infidelity. Pitt instantly guessed Rawdon intended to duel Steyne. Rawdon asked: "I must leave him to you and Jane, Pitt--only it will be a comfort to me if you will promise me to be his friend."

**Financial Settlement (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon drew pocket-book found in Becky's desk: "Here's six hundred--I want you to give the money to Briggs, who lent it to us--and who was kind to the boy--and I've always felt ashamed of having taken the poor old woman's money. And here's some more--I've only kept back a few pounds--which Becky may as well have." Thousand-pound note fell out.

**Challenge to Steyne (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon knocked at Gaunt House, handed card to purple Silenus porter: "Colonel Crawley would be all day after one o'clock at the Regent Club in St. James's Street--not at home." Proceeded to Knightsbridge Barracks.

**Meeting with Captain Macmurdo (Chapter 23)**: Rawdon reached Knightsbridge on Sunday morning and found Captain Macmurdo at home in barracks. Macmurdo (age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, best shots and riders in England, Rawdon's former rival, Waterloo veteran) was reading Bell's Life. Macmurdo knew duel arrangements perfectly—"common refuge of gentlemen in trouble."

**Macmurdo's Role as Second (Chapter 23)**: Composed letter to Steyne on behalf of Colonel Rawdon Crawley requesting appointment of friend to arrange meeting "with as little delay as possible." Letter delivered via Macmurdo's servant to Regent Club.

**Rawdon's Emotional Revelation (Chapter 23)**: Covered face with hands, overcome: "You don't know how fond I was of that one...I followed her like a footman. I gave up everything I had to her. I'm a beggar because I would marry her. By Jove, sir, I've pawned my own watch in order to get her anything she fancied; and she--she's been making a purse for herself all the time, and grudged me a hundred pound to get me out of quod." Showed Macmurdo thousand-pound note as evidence of Rebecca's guilt and selfishness.

**Rawdon's Paternal Concern (Chapter 23)**: "He's a regular trump, that boy...I say, Mac, if anything goes wrong--if I drop--I should like you to--to go and see him, you know, and say that I was very fond of him...give him these gold sleeve-buttons: it's all I've got." Covered face with black hands, tears rolled.

**Preparation for Duel (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1376)**: Macmurdo ordered breakfast with cheerful voice—"devilled kidneys and a herring." Offered Rawdon clean clothes from own wardrobe ("we were always pretty much of a size, Rawdon, my boy"). Rawdon dressed while Macmurdo continued reading Bell's Life. Macmurdo then performed his own toilette with particular care: waxed mustachios into brilliant polish, put on tight cravat and buff waistcoat. Young officers at mess-room breakfast complimented Mac on appearance and joked he was "going to be married that Sunday"—referring, obliquely, to the duel protocol.

## The Dissolution of Curzon Street Household (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1375–1383)

**Mademoiselle Fifine's Abandonment and Theft (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1375–1380)**: Rawdon's servant reported: "There's a regular shinty in the house, and everything at sixes and sevens. The landlord's come in and took possession." When Rebecca rang for her maid Mademoiselle Fifine in afternoon, maid did not appear. 

**Fifine's Escape**: Fifine had quit premises hours before "on French leave." After picking up trinkets from drawing-room, Fifine packed her own boxes in her apartment, called cab herself, brought down trunks single-handed without aid from other servants (who hated her), and departed Curzon Street without saying goodbye to anyone. "The game, in her opinion, was over in that little domestic establishment."

**Fifine's Thefts**: Beyond her own property, Fifine secured items belonging to Rebecca: four richly gilt Louis Quatorze candlesticks, six gilt albums, keepsakes, Books of Beauty, gold enamelled snuff-box once belonging to Madame du Barri, sweetest little inkstand and mother-of-pearl blotting book (which Becky used for charming pink notes), and all silver laid on table for small entertainment Rawdon had interrupted. She left behind: plated ware, fire irons, chimney-glasses, and rosewood cottage piano (too cumbrous).

**Fifine's Later Life (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1380)**: Subsequently kept milliner's shop in Rue du Helder, Paris, under name Madame de Saint-Amaranthe, living "with great credit" and enjoying patronage of Lord Steyne. Always spoke of England "as of the most treacherous country in the world" and claimed she had been "affreusement volé by natives of that island." "May she flourish as she deserves--she appears no more in our quarter of Vanity Fair."

**Household Mutiny (Chapter 23 – Excerpts 1381–1383)**: When Rebecca, in white cashmere dressing-gown, entered drawing-room after ringing unanswered, found: cook with blackened face seated on chintz sofa beside Mrs. Raggles, administering Maraschino; page with sugar-loaf buttons putting fingers in cream dish; footman talking to Raggles (face full of perplexity and woe); servants entirely indifferent to Rebecca's calls. None obeyed though door was open and Becky had screamed multiple times.

**Cook's Rebellion (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1382)**: Cook defiantly drank Maraschino, declaring: "YOUR sofy, indeed! I'm a settin' on Mrs. Raggles's sofy...which they bought with honest money...And I'm thinkin' if I set here until I'm paid my wages, I shall set a precious long time...set I will, too--ha! ha!" Servants burst into laughter; Raggles maintained "most melancholy countenance" and did not join.

**Trotter's Accusation (Chapter 23 – Excerpt 1383)**: Footman Trotter, flushed and inebriated from "vinous stimulus," announced: "He ain't a coming back...He sent for his things, and I wouldn't let 'em go, although Mr. Raggles would; and I don't b'lieve he's no more a Colonel than I am. He's hoff, and I suppose you're a goin' after him. You're no better than swindlers, both on you. Don't be a bullyin' ME. I won't stand it. Pay us our selleries, I say." Simpson the page, "affected by his mistress's deplorable situation," prevented Trotter from further outrage but Trotter's sentiment stood unchallenged.

## Key Relationships and Character States

**Rawdon**: Complete moral regeneration. Transformed from spendthrift to responsible father. Prepared for death; entrusted son to Pitt and Jane; settled debts using Steyne's money; now arranging duel as matter of honor. Emotional depth revealed: profound love for Rebecca now revealed as misplaced; genuine paternal affection for little Rawdon strong and genuine. Has become Macmurdo's client for duel arrangements. Currently at Knightsbridge Barracks with Macmurdo, dressed and ready, awaiting Steyne's response.

**Rebecca**: Utterly ruined. Exposed as Steyne's paid mistress. Husband gone forever. Curzon Street household in chaos—landlord taken possession, servants drunk and mutinous, wages unpaid. Maid fled with valuable plunder. Facing scandal, destitution, and abandonment. Recovery impossible.

**Steyne**: Exposed as financial corruptor and seducer. Scarred by Rawdon's assault; wore scar to dying day. Has received challenge via Macmurdo. Awaits response through appointed second. Continuing to support Fifine in Paris as Madame de Saint-Amaranthe.

**Pitt and Lady Jane**: Jane rescued Rawdon from spunging-house; entrusted with little Rawdon's guardianship should Rawdon die. Pitt refuses financial help; all money tied up. Promised hundred pounds to lawyer tomorrow. Will receive six hundred pounds (from Steyne's money via Rawdon) for Briggs and little Rawdon's care.

**Little Rawdon**: At school; being initiated into Latin Grammar. Happy and laughing in black gown and breeches. Will receive six hundred pounds and gold sleeve-buttons (Rawdon's gift) if Rawdon dies.

**Amelia**: Continued anguish. Separated from son; son indifferent to separation. Care-worn, sad, sleeps little, weeps and prays. Evening vigils at Russell Square.

**Captain Macmurdo**: Age nearly fifty, twenty-four years in regiment, veteran of Waterloo, best shots and riders in England, former rival of Rawdon. "Common refuge of gentlemen in trouble." Conducting Rawdon's duel arrangements with care and professionalism. Has greatest regard from Royal Highness late Commander-in-Chief.

**Briggs**: Lent money to Rawdon and Rebecca; kind to little Rawdon. Will receive six hundred pounds from Rawdon via Pitt.

**Servants at Curzon Street**: Cook (blackened face, drunk on Maraschino); Simpson page (sugar-loaf buttons, young, affected by mistress's plight); Trotter footman (drunk, mutinous, accusing); Mrs. Raggles (receiving Maraschino from cook); other servants drinking, demanding wages unpaid.

**Mademoiselle Fifine**: French maid, accomplice to Rebecca's affair, in Steyne's pay. Has fled to Paris, opened milliner's shop as Madame de Saint-Amaranthe under Steyne's patronage. Stole four gilt candelabras, six albums, keepsakes, gold snuff-box, inkstand, blotting book, silver table service. "May she flourish as she deserves--she appears no more in our quarter of Vanity Fair."

**CRITICAL STATE**: Duel between Rawdon and Steyne formally initiated. Rawdon at Knightsbridge Barracks with Macmurdo, prepared for combat. Steyne has received challenge and presumably appointed second. Response awaited. Curzon Street household completely collapsed; Rebecca abandoned, surrounded by mutinous servants demanding unpaid wages; household property plundered by Fifine. Rawdon's son's future secured; debts to be settled from Steyne's money. All parties aware of duel's imminence: "as little delay as possible."
